basic_info.name: Open Nucleus (server)
basic_info.description: Open Nucleus is an open-source, offline-first electronic health record (EHR) system explicitly designed for zero-connectivity environments: military forward operating bases, disaster-relief zones and small clinics in sub-Saharan Africa. Its core thesis is that the Git repository is the source of truth and SQLite is only a rebuildable search index, so the system assumes no network and treats connectivity as a bonus. The single most load-bearing fact is its dual-layer encrypted data model: every clinical write goes through a validate -> extract search fields -> per-patient AES-256-GCM encrypt -> Git commit -> SQLite upsert pipeline, where each patient has a unique data encryption key (DEK) wrapped by a master key, and deleting that key produces crypto-erasure of all of the patient's FHIR data without rewriting Git history. It implements a FHIR R4 write/read pipeline across roughly 18 resource types, Ed25519 challenge-response auth with EdDSA JWTs and SMART on FHIR v2 scopes, a FHIR Consent-based consent-check middleware with time-limited (4h) break-glass emergency access, and a Git-based node-to-node sync with a FHIR-aware merge driver that classifies conflicts into auto-merge / review / block. It is a hackathon-stage open-source project (last commit 2026-03-29, 8 stars, 60 commits, 0 forks) rather than a clinically validated or production-deployed product, and it is an EHR data substrate rather than a clinical summary generator: it has no patient-elicited history module, no LLM summarization and no India/ABDM/NRCeS output contract.
basic_info.organization: Open Nucleus (GitHub organization), with the server repository authored by the GitHub user/contributor 'FibrinLab'. The LICENSE and README attribute the server to 'AGPLv3 - FibrinLab'. The GitHub org lists United Kingdom as its location, reports 2 followers and had no public members at verification time. The project is a small multi-repo ecosystem (server, open-anchor, open-sentinel, open-engram, open-pharm-dosing) with no company or institutional backing disclosed.
basic_info.country: United Kingdom (organization origin). Target deployment context is sub-Saharan Africa (military forward operating bases, disaster relief zones, small clinics). Not designed for or validated in India.
basic_info.status: Research / hackathon-stage open-source prototype; effectively dormant since 2026-03-29 (no commits, releases or tags in the ~5.5 months to 2026-09-16). Repository shows 60 commits, 8 stars, 0 forks, 0 open issues and 0 pull requests. The final commit message ('docs: IOTA-only README for MasterZ hackathon') indicates it was last shaped for a hackathon demo. It is not production and not clinically validated.

technical_features.what_it_does: Open Nucleus is an offline-first EHR server: it stores FHIR R4 resources as per-patient encrypted JSON files inside a Git repository, indexes a minimal subset of searchable fields in SQLite, and exposes REST plus FHIR REST APIs (reported ~95 REST + ~85 FHIR + 11 SMART endpoints) for patient, encounter, observation, condition, medication, allergy, immunization, procedure, consent, practitioner, organization, location and measure-report resources. It provides device authentication (Ed25519 challenge-response, EdDSA JWTs, bootstrap secrets), role-based access control for six roles, consent-gated access with break-glass, formulary/stock logic, integrity anchoring via Merkle roots, and peer-to-peer synchronisation via Git fetch/merge/push over ECDH-encrypted channels. Its relevance to Module C is architectural rather than functional: it demonstrates an offline, encrypted, standards-shaped clinical data pipeline with automatic provenance generation and crypto-erasure, but it does not perform conversational history-taking or summary generation - summarization and language-model reasoning live only in the separate optional open-sentinel surveillance agent (outbreak detection, not clinical summarization).
technical_features.architecture: Single Go binary monolith ('nucleus') with all services in-process: an HTTP server (chi router) behind a 9-stage middleware pipeline (rate limiter, request ID, JWT validator, consent check, RBAC enforcer, JSON schema validator, CORS, SMART v2 scope, audit logger). Business logic: patient write pipeline (validate -> assign meta -> extract search fields -> AES-256-GCM encrypt -> Git commit -> SQLite upsert -> auto-generate FHIR Provenance), auth (Ed25519), sync (FHIR-aware merge/conflict classification), formulary, and anchor (Merkle/DID/VC). Storage: a Git repository of encrypted FHIR JSON (source of truth, with a crypto.Mutex-serialized Git lock) plus a unified SQLite database used only as a rebuildable index (FTS5 full-text search, WAL mode, single writer). A Tauri v2 + React 19 + TypeScript desktop app is the practitioner client. Two optional side services: a Node.js IOTA Identity Bridge (@iota/identity-wasm, port 3001) for did:iota DIDs, W3C Verifiable Credentials and notarisation, and a Python 'Sentinel' clinical-surveillance agent over gRPC :50056 / HTTP :8090. Blockchain anchoring targets IOTA Rebased testnet via a deployed Move contract, with a fallback to a Hedera HCS backend. The project deliberately collapsed an earlier 5-microservice + gRPC gateway design into the monolith, claiming ~60% lower memory to fit a Raspberry Pi 4.
technical_features.inputs: FHIR R4 JSON resource bodies over REST (POST/PUT); practitioner device credentials and Ed25519 signatures for auth; FHIR Consent resources for access decisions; Git repositories and ECDH keys from peer nodes for synchronisation; WHO essential-medicines formulary data; for the optional Sentinel agent, imported seeded patient datasets (a cholera/measles outbreak demo scenario). No conversational audio, no patient dialogue, no OCR of documents and no patient-entered narrative are ingested anywhere in the core server.
technical_features.outputs: Stored and returned FHIR R4 resources (encrypted at rest in Git, decrypted on detail reads; search fields only on list reads); auto-generated FHIR Provenance resources (HL7 v3-DataOperation coding) attached to every clinical write; Git commit metadata; sync conflict records classified as auto-merge / review / block; Merkle roots and notarised hashes for integrity; at the ecosystem level, W3C Verifiable Credentials and did:iota identifiers; and Sentinel outbreak alerts derived from WHO IDSR thresholds. It does not emit a clinical summary Composition/Bundle, an HL7 IPS document, or any NRCeS/ABDM OPConsultRecord artifact.
technical_features.standards_compliance: Conformance is implementation-level and largely self-declared; there is no published profile-validation evidence. It uses FHIR R4 resource shapes and a custom per-resource structural validator (pkg/fhir/validate.go) across 17 resource types plus 5 'profiles', but does not claim validation against any named public Implementation Guide (no NRCeS FHIR IG, no HL7 IPS, no US Core). It implements SMART on FHIR v2 scope enforcement and a FHIR Consent-based access model. Automatic Provenance uses HL7 v3-DataOperation codes. Terminology use is limited: clinical codes are stored/indexed but there is no demonstrated SNOMED CT, LOINC, ICD or NAMASTE binding. Crypto claims (AES-256-GCM at rest, TLS in transit, Ed25519 signatures) are documented in SECURITY/PRIVACY. The PRIVACY.md compliance matrix targets GDPR, South Africa POPIA, Kenya DPA, Nigeria NDPA and HIPAA - not India's DPDP Act 2023 and not ABDM. Conformance is claimed in repo documentation, not independently audited or validated against a profile registry.
technical_features.offline_capability: Offline is the project's central design premise and its strongest technical contribution. Connectivity is not required to record, read or search data: FHIR JSON is committed locally to Git (source of truth) and SQLite is a pure local cache that can be rebuilt from Git if lost. Data at rest is encrypted per patient with AES-256-GCM using a per-patient DEK wrapped by a master key never written to disk; per-provider ECDH key grants allow revocation without re-encryption, and deleting a patient's key file yields crypto-erasure while preserving the Git hash chain. Nodes synchronise opportunistically via Git fetch/merge/push over ECDH-encrypted channels (Wi-Fi/BT/LAN discovery), with a FHIR-aware merge driver that classifies each conflict as auto-merge (latest timestamp), review (flag for clinician) or block (reject, safety-critical). Offline limitations are documented openly: Git commit messages and file paths are unencrypted (patient UUIDs can appear in commit metadata); blind HMAC-SHA256 indexes reduce but do not eliminate PII exposure (gender, clinical codes and resource IDs remain plaintext); and during sync there is a window in which a disconnected node that has not yet received a key-destruction commit may still hold a valid key. IOTA on-chain DID publication and anchoring require a funded/online account, so offline deployments fall back to did:key and local notarisation only.
technical_features.languages_supported: English only. All UI strings, documentation, note/field content and code identifiers are English; there is no evidence of Hindi, Devanagari-script rendering, code-mixed Hinglish, transliteration or any Indian-language support, and no bilingual output. [uncertain]
technical_features.deployment_model: Self-hosted edge/clinic-LAN deployment: a single Go binary plus a local Git repository and SQLite database running on practitioner hardware; ARCHITECTURE.md states the monolith was designed to fit a Raspberry Pi 4, and the practitioner client is a Tauri v2 desktop app (macOS .app / Windows .msi). Optional side processes are the Node.js IOTA identity bridge (port 3001) and the Python Sentinel agent (which needs 8GB+ RAM or connectivity for its LLM mode). A Dockerfile and commits referencing Render/Railway show a cloud-deployment path is also possible, but the intended mode is disconnected on-prem/edge. No GPU is required and no discrete-GPU or cloud-inference requirement is stated. No kiosk-mode touch UI and no patient-facing deployment model are provided.

performance_metrics.accuracy_or_quality_metrics: No clinical quality, accuracy, F1, ROUGE, BERTScore, concept-recall or error-rate figures are published anywhere in the repository or documentation. Quality evidence is limited to software correctness: Go unit/integration tests with race detection (patient, FHIR, gitstore, sqliteindex, auth, sync/merge, formulary, anchor, FHIR handlers), a 27-step interactive smoke test, and JSON-schema validation of written FHIR bodies. There is no evaluation of summary quality (there is no summarizer), no comparison against clinician notes, and no clinical validation study.
performance_metrics.latency: No latency, throughput or time-to-operation benchmarks are published. The only performance-oriented statements are architectural: the monolith removes five gRPC round-trips per request and is claimed to reduce memory footprint by ~60% versus the prior microservice design, and steps 5-6 of the write path are serialized by a mutex to prevent concurrent Git writes (steps 1-4 run outside the lock). Git commit-per-write is inherently heavier than a pure database write, but no measured write/read latency is given.
performance_metrics.resource_requirements: Documented target is low-resource edge hardware: the monolith was engineered to run on a Raspberry Pi 4, with ~60% claimed memory reduction versus the original 5-service + gateway architecture. Storage is a local Git repository plus one SQLite database (single-writer, WAL). No explicit RAM/CPU/storage numbers, and no GPU requirement. The optional Sentinel agent is the exception: its LLM mode needs connectivity or 8GB+ RAM, while its rule-based WHO IDSR mode runs offline. The project does not publish a footprint measurement for a 4GB CPU/iGPU kiosk.
performance_metrics.scale_metrics: Very small. GitHub metrics at verification: 8 stars, 0 forks, 0 watchers shown beyond 1, 60 commits, 0 open issues, 0 pull requests, no releases and no tags. Organization (Open Nucleus) has 6 repositories totals across the ecosystem, 2 followers and no public members. Demonstration scale is the seeded dataset: 6 patients plus a cholera/measles outbreak scenario. No user, clinic, record or transaction volumes are reported, and there is no production adoption evidence.
performance_metrics.evaluation_protocol: Software-engineering verification only, not clinical or benchmark evaluation: Go test suites across services with the race detector, a 27-step interactive smoke test (make smoke), schema validation of FHIR request bodies, and an end-to-end/test/e2e directory. There is no dataset, no metric, no clinician review, no peer-reviewed study and no reproducibility pack for any clinical or performance claim. All standards and security claims are vendor/author-claimed in documentation rather than externally validated.

milestone_significance.relevance_to_module_c: Open Nucleus is a strong architectural comparator for the offline-plus-encryption-plus-consent-plus-sync requirements that constrain MediKiosk Module C, even though it is functionally on the opposite side of the pipeline (it is an offline EHR substrate, not a summary generator). Three things are directly load-bearing. First, it is a working demonstration that an offline-first clinical system can treat a local Git repository as source of truth and a rebuildable SQLite index as a cache, which is the same offline-resilience discipline Module C needs for its summary store and for any future HIS/ABDM writeback. Second, it shows a clean per-patient envelope-encryption and crypto-erasure pattern (unique AES-256-GCM DEK per patient, master-key wrap, per-provider ECDH key grants with revocation, key destruction as the erasure primitive) that maps directly onto MediKiosk's DPDP Act 2023 right-to-erasure and India-residency requirements. Third, and most relevant to Module C's per-field provenance and physician-attestation goals, it auto-generates a FHIR Provenance resource on every write and enforces consent through middleware with an explicit, auditable break-glass path. Critically, it also shows the boundary MediKiosk must not cross: Open Nucleus is a data-integrity and storage system with no elicitation, no summarization and no NRCeS/ABDM contract, which is precisely the layer Module C owns.
milestone_significance.what_to_adopt_or_reject: Adopt: (1) the envelope-encryption/krypto-erasure design - per-patient AES-256-GCM DEK wrapped by a master key, per-provider ECDH key grants, key destruction as the deletion mechanism, because it satisfies DPDP right-to-erasure without rewriting data and keeps India-resident keys local; (2) automatic FHIR Provenance generation on every write and the idea of machine-readable per-resource provenance, extended for Module C to per-field provenance linking each summary field to its source utterance or digitized document; (3) consent-gated access middleware with an auditable, time-limited emergency break-glass and consent exportable for offline verification, which is the shape ABDM consent artifacts could take on a disconnected kiosk; (4) the three-tier sync/merge conflict classification (auto-merge by timestamp, review by clinician, block on safety-critical conflict) as a model for reconciling a kiosk-created summary with an existing record; (5) Git/append-only history as a tamper-evident audit trail. Reject or adapt: (1) blockchain anchoring (IOTA Rebased / Hedera HCS) - it adds connectivity dependence, unfamiliar operational risk and no ABDM/India procurement path, and ABDM's own consent-artefact and audit model is the sanctioned mechanism; (2) storing full clinical payloads only as opaque ciphertext when Module C needs a field-level, physician-legible provenance view; (3) the unencrypted Git commit metadata and plaintext index fields (gender, codes, UUIDs) - unacceptable for a patient-facing OPD context; (4) its near-absent consent workflow (PRIVACY.md states no consent management system in V1, relying on clinician professional judgment) - MediKiosk requires explicit patient consent captured before processing; (5) AGPL-3.0 code reuse in a kiosk product (see business_info.license); (6) the assumption that a patient record already exists - Module C must synthesise a record where none exists.
milestone_significance.limitations_and_risks: Open Nucleus is not production software and not clinically validated: it is a 60-commit hackathon-stage project whose last commit was 2026-03-29 (dormant ~5.5 months), with 8 stars, 0 forks and no releases. It has no clinical quality evaluation, no peer review and no external security audit - its crypto, standards and compliance claims are author-claimed in README/PRIVACY/SECURITY files. Its documented limitations are material: Git commit metadata and file paths are unencrypted and can expose patient UUIDs; blind indexes leave gender, clinical codes and IDs in plaintext; sync can leave a window where a disconnected node still holds a key after erasure; and on-chain DID anchoring requires a funded network account. Its standards story is thin - custom FHIR R4 validation with no named IG, no SNOMED/LOINC/ICD/NAMASTE binding, no HL7 IPS, and a privacy posture aimed at GDPR/POPIA/Kenya/NDPA/HIPAA rather than India's DPDP Act or ABDM. Consent is explicitly not a V1 capability, contradicting the README's headline 'consent-based access control' framing and reducing the usefulness of its consent comparison. Licensing is a real risk: the server is AGPL-3.0 (network copyleft), so any reuse inside a kiosk product would impose source-disclosure obligations. The optional Sentinel agent's LLM mode needs connectivity or 8GB+ RAM, so its 'offline AI' claim is only partly true. Nothing here addresses elicitation, bilingual summary generation, NRCeS OPConsultRecord emission, or India data residency.
milestone_significance.differentiator_vs_medikiosk: Open Nucleus and MediKiosk Module C are complementary, not competing: Open Nucleus is the offline encrypted record substrate; Module C is the patient-elicited, physician-ready summary producer. Open Nucleus strengthens MediKiosk's differentiation by supplying a credible, openly readable reference for the offline + encryption + sync + provenance spine that MediKiosk also needs, and by validating that zero-connectivity EHR operation is technically tractable. It does not erode any of MediKiosk's stated differentiators: it emits no NRCeS/ABDM OPConsultRecord, has no bilingual Hindi/English output, no conversational elicitation, no document digitization summary, no India data-residency story and no ABDM HIP/HIU/PHR role. If anything, it clarifies the gap: the offline substrate problem is solved in open source, so MediKiosk's defensible value sits one layer up - structured, provenance-tracked, NRCeS-conformant bilingual summary generation for a patient who has no prior digital record. The two ideas worth explicitly mirroring are crypto-erasure as the DPDP right-to-erasure mechanism and automatic provenance-as-a-first-class-resource.

business_info.license: GNU Affero General Public License v3.0 (AGPL-3.0) for the server repository, with the README and LICENSE attributing it to 'AGPLv3 - FibrinLab'. AGPL-3.0 is a strong network-copyleft license: if the software is modified and offered over a network, the corresponding source must be offered to users. Sibling ecosystem repositories are more permissive: open-anchor, open-sentinel, open-engram and open-pharm-dosing are Apache-2.0. This mixed licensing matters because any reuse of the server code inside a kiosk product would carry AGPL obligations, whereas the Apache-2.0 libraries are safe to vendor.
business_info.pricing: None. The software is free to download and self-host under AGPL-3.0; there is no paid tier, support contract, hosted offering or enterprise plan.
business_info.funding: [uncertain] No funding, grants, sponsorships, corporate backing or commercial entity are disclosed anywhere in the repository, organization or documentation. The project appears to be an unfunded volunteer/hackathon effort (the last commit references a 'MasterZ hackathon').
business_info.commercial_status: Non-commercial, unpaid open-source project. No commercial product, no vendor, no sales motion and no government or NGO procurement is evidenced. There is no support commitment and no release cadence; the project has been dormant since 2026-03-29.

competition_ecosystem.competitors: In the offline-first / low-connectivity health-record space, comparable open-source systems include OpenMRS (and its offline/sync modules), Bahmni and IHospital, LibreHealth, OpenELIS, DHIS2 for aggregate data, and mHealth/CHW platforms such as Medic's Community Health Toolkit, CommCare and Intelehealth. On the India ABDM-plus-offline axis the closest comparator is CureNet (labishbardiya/CureNet), an offline-first ABDM-oriented FHIR R4 platform with local AES-256-GCM storage, which overlaps MediKiosk far more directly than Open Nucleus does. Open Nucleus does not compete with MediKiosk Module C at all in function - no summarization, no elicitation, no India interoperability - but it competes in the narrower sense of being an alternative open-source base a kiosk project might adopt for storage/encryption instead of building its own.
competition_ecosystem.integrations: IOTA Rebased testnet (deployed Move 'anchoring' smart contract, package 0x415ad713...; did:iota DIDs, W3C VCs, notarisation via the open-anchor Node.js identity bridge) and a Hedera HCS/HTS anchoring path referenced in commits. Standards integrations are SMART on FHIR v2 and FHIR Consent. Clinical/operational integrations are a WHO essential-medicines formulary with drug-interaction logic and an open-pharm-dosing library for FHIR R4 Timing. Client/hosting integrations are a Tauri desktop app, Docker, and Render/Railway cloud deployment. There are no HIS/EHR vendor integrations, no ABDM gateway roles (HIP/HIU/PHR), no Indian Health Locker integration and no Indian health-system integrations of any kind.
competition_ecosystem.ecosystem_notes: Open Nucleus is evidence that offline-first, standards-shaped health records with strong local encryption are an active open-source design pattern, driven by humanitarian/military/disaster use cases where connectivity cannot be assumed. That is directly analogous to MediKiosk's offline-first hard constraint, so adopting similar storage/encryption/consent patterns is low-risk and well-precedented. The blockchain-anchoring framing (IOTA/Hedera) is the part most likely to conflict with Indian government procurements, where ABDM's own consent-artefact, audit and Health Locker mechanisms are the sanctioned interoperability rails; a kiosk should stay on ABDM rails rather than introduce a third-party distributed ledger. The AGPL-3.0 server license also means Indian integrators cannot simply fork it into a proprietary product without releasing source, which likely limits its adoption in commercial HIS/kiosk settings. Finally, the project's dormancy (no activity since March 2026) means it should be treated as a design reference to learn from, not a maintained dependency to build on.

history.release_date: [uncertain] No formal release, version tag or first-publication date is published; the repository has no releases or tags. Visible commit history in the current window begins 2026-03-03, but earlier commits are referenced (the history page paginates beyond what was fetched), so the project was almost certainly created in late February or early March 2026.
history.key_milestones: 2026-03-03: SMART on FHIR phase implemented and stale README claims corrected. 2026-03-09 to 2026-03-10: 'Overhaul' phases - collapsed the 5-service + gRPC gateway into a single Go monolith, implemented per-patient encryption and crypto-erasure, replaced broken sync crypto with ECDH key exchange, and added IPEHR-inspired access control with encrypted/blind indexes. 2026-03-17 to 2026-03-18: built the desktop app first in Flutter (HTTP client, dashboard, patient detail with 10-tab clinical view, sync/conflicts, alerts, anchor, consent, settings screens, tests). 2026-03-21 to 2026-03-22: demo-readiness work integrating open-anchor and open-pharm-dosing, adding Hedera HCS anchoring and IOTA Rebased dual-blockchain support, then rewriting the desktop app from Flutter to Tauri + React. 2026-03-23: Dockerfile and Render/Railway deployment packaging. 2026-03-29: final commits wiring the IOTA Identity bridge into the server and replacing the README with an 'IOTA-only README for MasterZ hackathon'. No further activity through 2026-09-16.
history.recent_changes_last_6_months: The six-month window (mid-March to mid-September 2026) contains only the tail of the project's burst: all commits fall in March 2026, with the last on 2026-03-29. Those final changes added the IOTA Identity SDK bridge (did:iota DIDs, W3C Verifiable Credentials, notarisation) into the server, configured the deployed IOTA testnet Move contract package ID, and re-oriented the README for the MasterZ hackathon. Nothing has changed since - no commits, no releases, no issues or PR activity - so the currency check is negative: Open Nucleus is a frozen March-2026 snapshot, not a moving target. This means its architecture can be cited as stable prior art but its claims have not been refreshed and any defects documented at that time remain.

market_positioning.target_users: Primary users are frontline clinicians, community health workers, nurses and site/regional administrators operating in austere, disconnected settings: military forward operating bases, disaster-relief field clinics, and small clinics in sub-Saharan Africa. Secondary audiences are NGOs, humanitarian-health organisations and developers/integrators who need an offline, encrypted, FHIR-shaped record store to build on. It is practitioner-side and administrator-side infrastructure; patients are not direct users and there is no patient-facing intake experience.
market_positioning.market_segment: Offline-first electronic health records / low-resource clinical data infrastructure, alongside FHIR tooling and health-data synchronisation-and-integrity middleware. It is not in the intake, ambient-scribing, summary-generation or AYUSH-software segments that MediKiosk Module C occupies.
market_positioning.positioning_statement: The project pitches itself in its own words as 'Open-source, offline-first electronic health record (EHR) system for military forward operating bases, disaster relief zones, and small clinics in sub-Saharan Africa. Assumes zero connectivity as the default and treats network access as a bonus.' Its organization tagline is 'Open Nucleus is an open-source, offline-first electronic health record (EHR) system designed small clinics in Africa.' The documented value proposition rests on the dual-layer encrypted Git/SQLite data model, per-patient AES-256-GCM encryption with crypto-erasure, consent-based access control, blind indexes, and IOTA-based tamper-evidence - framed around data integrity, privacy and zero-connectivity resilience rather than clinical intelligence.
